text: Same letter, same sound: Χριστός has both — λόγος has only the final one.
finding: This is the claim the whole prose register grew out of — λόγος was once said to have both sigmas and has only the final one. It now carries data-has="σς", and check_lessons fails if the word named does not contain both characters.

text: Every word starting with a vowel carries a mark.
finding: 63,625 vowel-initial tokens in the SBLGNT, 63,625 with a breathing. The first pass reported eight exceptions and every one was a diphthong -- in αυ, ευ, ου, ει the breathing sits on the SECOND vowel, and the detector read only the first. The claim was true and the check was wrong.

text: It is the only chapter where that is true.
finding: A claim about the course's own shape — chapter 1 being the only one whose content is the writing system rather than the language. True of the app as built.

text: Three rules that trip people up Sigma is written ς at the end of a word and σ everywhere else.
finding: Exact, both ways round, across all 137,554 tokens: ς never appears anywhere but the last letter, and σ never appears as the last letter. Not one exception either way.

text: It is not pronounced, but it usually signals the dative case — about five times in six.
finding: 7,481 tokens carry an iota subscript; 6,268 are dative = 83.8%, against 83.3% for five-in-six. And 'the main exception is subjunctive endings' holds: 784 of the 1,213 non-datives are subjunctives, 65% of them, comfortably the largest class. The rest are lexical — Ἡρῴδης, λῃστής, λάθρᾳ.

text: One letter, one sound — Χριστός has both.
finding: The claim the register grew out of. Χριστός contains both σ and ς; λόγος has only the final one. Held now by check_lessons through data-has="σς".

text: This catches everyone at least once: Σὺ εἶ ὁ ἐρχόμενος ἢ ἕτερον προσδοκῶμεν; "Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?" John's disciples are asking a question, and the only thing on the page that tells you so is that final mark.
finding: The Greek question mark. The verse is held to the text by check_lessons; the claim about what catches people is pedagogy. Read and left as written.

text: Dative, about five times in six.
finding: 6,268 of the 7,481 iota subscripts are dative: 83.8% against 83.3% for five in six.

text: The accent is the only difference between them.
finding: τίς against τις: 554 and 530, identical in every letter. The corpus keeps them apart as separate lemmas, which is the chapter's point.

text: Accents Greek has three accents: acute ( ά ), grave ( ὰ ) and circumflex ( ᾶ ).
finding: Three distinct accent marks are in use in the corpus and no others: acute, grave and circumflex.

text: There are twenty-four letters and you already know several of them.
finding: Twenty-five distinct letter characters occur, which is the twenty-four letters plus the final sigma ς — exactly what the chapter's next rule is about.

text: Initial ῥ always takes the rough breathing, though it is generally not sounded as an h: ῥῆμα is rhēma , near enough rēma .
finding: 231 of 233 rho-initial tokens carry the rough breathing. The two that do not are the same word: Ραββουνι, Mark 10:51 and John 20:16, a transliterated Aramaic address that SBLGNT writes bare. True of Greek words, and 'always' is a word a learner will take literally when they meet Ραββουνι.

text: If you cannot pronounce it, you cannot hold it in your memory, and a word you cannot hold is a word you will meet as a stranger every time.
finding: Pedagogy, not a claim about Greek. Read and left as written.

text: Some are ours exactly, some are ours in disguise, and only a handful are genuinely new.
finding: About the alphabet's familiarity. Read and left as written.

text: The optative is rarer still, and by the Koine period it is fading: 68 occurrences in the whole New Testament.
finding: 68 optatives in the SBLGNT, exact.

text: Only the verb and the sentence can.
finding: The middle/passive caution, which the outside audit singled out as one of the course's best instincts. Read and left as written.

text: Time is only fixed in the indicative Outside the indicative mood, the tense is telling you about aspect and almost nothing about time.
finding: SOURCED. Robertson, Grammar ch.XVIII (Tense): "The Greeks evidently felt that there was no need for time in the other modes except in a relative sense. As a matter of fact, the real time of subjunctive, optative, and imperative is future in relation to speaker or writer... It is only by the augment (probably an adverb) that past time is clearly expressed" — and later, "There is no time element in the present subjunctive." So the augment really is the temporal element, and what time a non-indicative carries is relative. Chapter 2's 'almost nothing about time' is the right strength; chapter 16's 'aspect and nothing more' was the overstatement this pass corrected. Read from the clean Logos export in Greek App Reference/Robertson, not the broken OCR.

text: Every finite Greek verb form encodes person, number, tense, voice and mood in one word.
finding: True as stated, because it says FINITE. The chapter's body did not: it opened 'Every Greek verb form encodes five things', twenty lines above its own 'The infinitive and the participle ... decline to specify a person at all'. Corpus: participles 6,640 plus infinitives 2,285 are 8,925 of 28,056 verb forms, 32%. The body now scopes it and names the exception; this quiz explanation always had it right. Found by reading.

text: Two sets of endings Primary endings appear on the tenses whose indicative refers to present or future time: present, future, perfect.
finding: The traditional primary/secondary division: primary on present, future and perfect, secondary on imperfect, aorist and pluperfect. Standard, and the corpus's own endings bear it out.

text: The practical difficulty is that middle and passive share their endings in most tenses, so the form alone often cannot tell you which one is meant.
finding: The chapter's thesis about voice, and true of the present, imperfect, perfect and pluperfect.

text: Four out of five verbs that carry a person and a number are indicative, and the whole of chapters 3 to 16 stays inside it.
finding: 15,589 indicatives of 19,131 finite forms = 81.5%. The scoping — 'that carry a person and a number' — is exactly right, which is what made the unscoped claim earlier in the chapter stand out.

text: Only the indicative fixes time.
finding: Sourced to Robertson ch.XVIII: outside the indicative there is no need for time 'except in a relative sense', and only the augment expresses past time.

text: Only the indicative fixes time, which is why the tense of a participle tells you about aspect and not about when.
finding: SOURCED. Robertson, Grammar ch.XVIII (Tense): "The Greeks evidently felt that there was no need for time in the other modes except in a relative sense. As a matter of fact, the real time of subjunctive, optative, and imperative is future in relation to speaker or writer... It is only by the augment (probably an adverb) that past time is clearly expressed" — and later, "There is no time element in the present subjunctive." So the augment really is the temporal element, and what time a non-indicative carries is relative. Chapter 2's 'almost nothing about time' is the right strength; chapter 16's 'aspect and nothing more' was the overstatement this pass corrected. Read from the clean Logos export in Greek App Reference/Robertson, not the broken OCR.

text: It lives in the principal parts of a few hundred verbs, and the commonest of those you will meet often enough to learn without trying.
finding: About irregularity. Twenty-one verbs show all six parts in the corpus and many hundreds show some; 'a few hundred' is fair. Read and left as written.

text: The endings are shared in most tenses, so only the verb and the sentence can settle it.
finding: Read and left as written.

text: Principal parts Each verb has up to six principal parts — the building blocks every other form is made from: present, future, aorist active, perfect active, perfect middle/passive, aorist passive.
finding: Twenty-one verbs in the corpus have all six attested — αἴρω, βάλλω, γεννάω, γράφω, δέω, δίδωμι among them — so 'up to six' is right and the six categories the chapter names are the ones the text actually fills.

text: The discipline From here on, never say a form means something until you have parsed it.
finding: The course's own working rule, not a claim about the language. Read and left as written — and it is the rule this whole audit has been applying.

text: Only in the indicative.
finding: Same, and the augment is indicative-only.

text: Mark does it constantly, and most English translations quietly convert it — so if you have only read this in English you have never seen it.
finding: The quiz twin of the historical-present claim recorded as unsettled in the body: at Mark 1:40 the six reference translations split three and three, and four of the six are old and deliberately literal, so they cannot establish a majority. The claim is very likely right about the versions a reader holds; this library cannot show it.

text: Singular Plural 1st εἰμί ἐσμέν 2nd εἶ ἐστέ 3rd ἐστί(ν) εἰσί(ν) οὐκ ἔστιν ὧδε, ἠγέρθη γὰρ "He is not here, for he has been raised." Two verbs, and between them most of chapter 2: ἔστιν is present, ἠγέρθη is aorist passive with its augment showing.
finding: All six forms of the present indicative of εἰμί are attested: εἰμί 45, εἶ 92, ἐστίν 176, ἐσμέν 21, ἐστέ 25, εἰσίν 69. And the verse beside it is exactly as described — ἔστιν present, ἠγέρθη aorist passive with its augment.

text: It is why the grid drill exists, and why filling the table in from memory is worth more than reading it ten times.
finding: A claim about the app rather than about Greek: the grid drill does exist, js/grid.js derives 45 rounds from the paradigm tables, and check_grids holds the derivation. True as a statement about the product.

text: He does this constantly, and most English translations quietly convert it to a past tense — so if you have only ever read this in English, you have never seen it.
finding: NOT SETTLED by the app's own six, and worth recording why. Mark 1:40 Καὶ ἔρχεται πρὸς αὐτὸν λεπρός: KJV 'there came a leper', BSB 'a leper came' and NHEB 'A leper came' convert to the past; ASV 'there cometh', Darby 'there comes' and YLT 'doth come' keep the present. Three of six. But the six are ASV, BSB, Darby, KJV, YLT and NHEB — four of them old and deliberately literal — so they are a good set for refuting an 'every' or 'no translation' claim and a poor sample for 'most translations'. The modern versions a reader is likely to hold (NIV, ESV, NASB, CSB) do overwhelmingly convert, which is what the sentence means, but this library cannot demonstrate it. Needs a modern translation or a reader who has one.

text: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ ἄρτος τῆς ζωῆς "I am the bread of life." Here the pronoun ἐγώ is written out, even though εἰμι already says I.
finding: John 6:35, with ἐγώ written out though εἰμι already carries the person. Read and left as written.

text: That division holds about nine times in ten, and the commonest exception earns its keep.
finding: Corpus: οὐ stands before an indicative 1,328 of 1,486 = 89%; μή before a non-indicative 828 of 938 = 88%. So 'μή with everything else' is a strong tendency, not a rule: 73 bare μή + indicative, mostly the interrogative μή expecting the answer no, plus 21 εἰ μή and 16 οὐ μή. John 21:5 added as the example, where the text supplies the expected Οὔ in the next clause.

text: None of these is a different tense.
finding: About the three uses of the present. Read and left as written.

text: They decline exactly like λόγος , and only the article tells you they are feminine at all.
finding: ἡ ὁδός and ἡ ἔρημος: second-declension endings with the feminine article. Read and left as written.

text: Nouns fall into three declensions, which are just three patterns of endings.
finding: Three declensions is the standard division and the one Abbott-Smith's genitives sort every noun into — 690 first, 558 second, 587 third.

text: In the plural it is identical to the nominative, but in the second declension singular it ends in -ε.
finding: 207 second-declension vocative singulars end -ε; the two that do not are the nominative doing vocative duty, at Acts 7:42 and Philippians 4:1.

text: It agrees with its noun in gender, number and case, which means that once you know the article you can read the case of almost any noun attached to one, even a noun you have never met.
finding: Standard agreement, and the seventeen article forms make it the reading aid the chapter says it is.

text: Learn every noun in that full form from the first day.
finding: Advice. Read and left as written.

text: It is -ων in every gender and every declension, which makes it easy to spot and useless for gender.
finding: 3,321 genitive plurals in the corpus; the 76 that do not end -ων are all indeclinable numerals — δώδεκα, δύο, ἑπτά, τριάκοντα, ὀγδοήκοντα — which do not inflect at all.

text: Every other ending is identical.
finding: Confirmed from λόγος and ἔργον side by side: they differ only in the nominative and accusative.

text: And the dative singular ends in a long vowel with an iota written underneath it: λόγῳ , ἔργῳ .
finding: λόγῳ 45 and ἔργῳ 10, both with the subscript, both attested.

text: Those are tendencies rather than rules, as the next two verses show.
finding: The chapter's own framing of the article, and the framing this pass had to extend to the PRESENCE of the article as well as its absence when Luke 18:13 was settled.

text: Every one of the eight is distinct, which is what makes the second declension the place to start.
finding: λόγος has eight case/number slots and all eight are spelled differently in the corpus: λόγος, λόγου, λόγῳ, λόγον, λόγοι, λόγων, λόγοις, λόγους.

text: 668 of them in the New Testament.
finding: Quiz explanation restating a body claim already settled in this chapter, and it restates it faithfully: "There is a fifth: the vocative , used for addressing someone directly, and it occurs 668 times.". Two things hold it there — the body claim is verified against the corpus, and check_quiz fails on a quiz number that disagrees with the body's, which is the fault that put δίδωσιν at 11 in one section and 10 in the next.

text: Watch only the ending.
finding: An instruction for reading the three λόγος examples. Read and left.

text: A noun in apposition to a pronoun regularly takes the article, and Luke writes ὑμῖν τοῖς Φαρισαίοις and ὑμῖν τοῖς πλουσίοις the same way six times over, meaning nothing more than "you Pharisees", "you rich".
finding: Verified when Luke 18:13 was settled: a dative pronoun with a noun in apposition occurs 12 times, 8 of them articular, and seven of the eight are Luke — ὑμῖν τοῖς πλουσίοις (6:24), ὑμῖν τοῖς Φαρισαίοις (11:42, 11:43), ὑμῖν τοῖς νομικοῖς (11:46, 11:52), ὑμῖν τοῖς φίλοις (12:4), and μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ itself.

text: ἔργον — neuter Singular Plural Nom ἔργον ἔργα Gen ἔργου ἔργων Dat ἔργῳ ἔργοις Acc ἔργον ἔργα Neuter differs from masculine only in the nominative and accusative, and in those two it has one form doing both jobs.
finding: ἔργον in the corpus: nominative singular ἔργον = accusative singular ἔργον, nominative plural ἔργα = accusative plural ἔργα, and the genitive and dative are ἔργου/ἔργῳ/ἔργων/ἔργοις, identical to λόγος. Exactly as stated.

text: λόγος on its own is a word or the word, and only the sentence decides.
finding: True and important: Greek has no indefinite article, so the anarthrous noun is genuinely ambiguous. Read and left as written.

text: Fourteen letters open by naming their writer ἀπόστολος or δοῦλος , and not one of the fourteen uses an article .
finding: Exactly fourteen, from the corpus: Romans, 1-2 Corinthians, Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, Colossians, 1-2 Timothy, Titus, James, 1-2 Peter, Jude. In every one the title word is anarthrous. 1-2 Thessalonians, Philemon and Hebrews open with no such title; 2-3 John use ὁ πρεσβύτερος, which is neither of the two words. Revelation 1:1 has articular δούλοις/δούλῳ, but there John is named in the third person and it is a title, not a greeting.

text: Seventeen forms, and they parse a quarter of the sentences you will read.
finding: Seventeen distinct spellings — ὁ ἡ τό τοῦ τῆς τῷ τῇ τόν τήν οἱ αἱ τά τῶν τοῖς ταῖς τούς τάς — filling 24 case/number/gender slots.

text: There is a fifth: the vocative , used for addressing someone directly, and it occurs 668 times.
finding: 668 vocatives in the SBLGNT, exact.

text: Only the sentence can tell you, and here μενεῖ needs a subject, so it is nominative.
finding: A worked reading of one verse. Read and left as written.

text: The definite article The article occurs 19,769 times in the New Testament — one word in every seven.
finding: 19,769 tokens carry lemma ὁ in the SBLGNT, against 137,554 tokens in all: one word in 6.96. A 19,770th token is tagged RA at Ephesians 2:13 but lemmatised ὅς, which is a MorphGNT edge case rather than the article.

text: What to watch for λόγων is genitive plural and so is ἔργων — the genitive plural is -ων in every gender and every declension you will meet.
finding: 3,321 genitive plurals in the corpus; 76 do not end -ων, and every one of those is an INDECLINABLE numeral — δώδεκα 23, δύο 13, ἑπτά 14, τριάκοντα, ὀγδοήκοντα — which MorphGNT tags with the case it functions in although the word does not inflect. Not a counterexample to a claim about declensions, and the sentence's 'you will meet' already scopes it.

text: In the plural the vocative is identical to the nominative, so it usually goes unnoticed; in the singular of the second declension it ends in -ε , and once you have seen it you will see it everywhere.
finding: 207 second-declension vocative singulars end -ε. Two do not, and both are the nominative form doing vocative duty rather than a vocative in -ος: οἶκος at Acts 7:42 and στέφανός at Philippians 4:1. The morphological claim stands; that idiom is a separate thing.

text: An absence tells you something only where the writer could have written it the other way.
finding: The course's own test, and the one that settled Luke 18:13 — where Luke could not have written it the other way.

text: Not one.
finding: Fourteen letters open by naming their writer ἀπόστολος or δοῦλος and the title word is anarthrous in every one.

text: Knowing its seventeen forms lets you read the case of almost any noun attached to one.
finding: Seventeen distinct spellings of the article occur, filling 24 case/number/gender slots.

text: Only there, and in those two it uses one form for both.
finding: ἔργον in the corpus: nominative singular = accusative singular = ἔργον, and nominative plural = accusative plural = ἔργα, while genitive and dative match λόγος exactly.

text: 19769 times, one word in every seven.
finding: Quiz explanation restating a body claim already settled in this chapter, and it restates it faithfully: "The definite article The article occurs 19,769 times in the New Testament — one word in every seven.". Two things hold it there — the body claim is verified against the corpus, and check_quiz fails on a quiz number that disagrees with the body's, which is the fault that put δίδωσιν at 11 in one section and 10 in the next.

text: ἐξ ἀνθρώπων δόξαν, οὔτε ἀφ’ ὑμῶν οὔτε ἀπ’ ἄλλων "glory from men, neither from you nor from others." Three of these in one line: ἐξ before a vowel, ἀφ’ before the rough breathing of ὑμῶν , and ἀπ’ before the smooth breathing of ἄλλων .
finding: The three elisions are on the page as described, and check_lessons holds the quotation to the verse it names.

text: If the stem ends in ε, ι or ρ , the alpha is kept all the way through: ἡμέρα, ἡμέρας, ἡμέρᾳ, ἡμέραν .
finding: The tendency is strong and not absolute. Among first-declension nouns whose lemma ends -α, the genitive singular is -ας 795 times against -ης 9 where the stem ends ε, ι or ρ, and -ης 97 against -ας 2 where it does not. So the rule predicts about 99% of the first group and 98% of the second.

text: ἐκ becomes ἐξ before a vowel: 679 times against 234 in the New Testament, so you will meet both, and the split is clean — every one of the 679 sits before a consonant and every one of the 234 before a vowel.
finding: Was '669 times against 227'. Both are CASE-SENSITIVE tallies: ἐκ is 669 lower-case plus 10 sentence-initial Ἐκ = 679, and ἐξ is 227 plus 7 Ἐξ = 234. check_claims' docstring names this exact fault — 'which is how seven undercounts got into the chapters: they were written from a case-sensitive tally' — and this was an eighth. Worse, check_claims had an IGNORE entry for the 227 whose stated reason was false: it called 227 'ἐκ's count', and ἐκ is 679. The corpus also settles the rule itself, which the sentence now says: all 679 ἐκ sit before a consonant and all 234 ἐξ before a vowel, with no exceptions either way. A sweep of every number-beside-a-Greek-word pair in all 27 chapters found no other instance of the fault.

text: Four prepositions worth meeting now A preposition tells you how its noun relates to the rest of the sentence, and in Greek it fixes that noun's case.
finding: ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ and ἀπό, each taking one case. Read and left as written.

text: Dative, always.
finding: ἐν takes the dative and nothing else — 2,730 of them, with the only apparent exceptions being my own test reaching past the indeclinable Ἰερουσαλήμ.

text: ὁ μαθητής , never ἡ μαθητής .
finding: All 262 occurrences of μαθητής are tagged masculine. Not one feminine.

text: It is one of the few accent rules worth learning as a rule, because it never varies and it identifies the form on sight.
finding: It never varies: all 298 first-declension common-noun genitive plurals in the New Testament end -ῶν with a circumflex, no exceptions.

text: ἐν, εἰς, ἐκ and ἀπό each take one case only, which makes them the most reliable case signposts in the text.
finding: True, with no real exceptions. ἐκ is 912 genitives and nothing else. ἐν, εἰς and ἀπό show a handful of apparent misses that are all my own test reaching past an indeclinable or a modifier — ἐν Ἰερουσαλήμ (indeclinable), εἰς ἀλεύρου σάτα where ἀλεύρου modifies the accusative σάτα, ἀπὸ τότε and ἀπ’ ἄρτι where the next word is an adverb.

text: The vowel depends on the letter before it, and the rule is worth knowing because it decides two of the four singular endings.
finding: The α/η rule in the first declension: after ε, ι or ρ the genitive is -ας 795 times against -ης 9; otherwise -ης 97 against -ας 2.

text: The genitive plural always has a circumflex Every first-declension noun ends its genitive plural in -ῶν , with a circumflex, wherever the accent falls in the rest of the word.
finding: 298 first-declension common-noun genitive plurals in the New Testament, and every one of them ends -ῶν with a circumflex. ZERO exceptions, so 'it never varies' in the next sentence is literally true. The only apparent counterexamples are place names — Σοδόμων, Ἱεροσολύμων, Γομόρρων, Θυατείρων — which are neuter plurals or otherwise not first-declension common nouns. Declension assigned from Abbott-Smith's genitives, the same classifier that settled chapter 17.

text: None of this changes the meaning or the case.
finding: About elision and the movable ν. Read and left as written.

text: Where the noun has no article, nothing decides it for you and the context is all you have — which is the same limit chapter 21 will reach with participles.
finding: The corrected sentence from this pass, and the limit chapter 21 reaches too. Read and left as written.

text: The article, and only the article.
finding: Now scoped in the body to 'wherever the noun has an article', which is where it is true.

text: This is why compound verbs are awkward to look up: the form no longer begins with the letters the lexicon lists.
finding: The quiz form of the same. Read and left as written.

text: ἔλυον is first singular or third plural, and you cannot tell from the word.
finding: Ten imperfect active forms are attested in the corpus as BOTH first singular and third plural of the same verb: ἔλεγον, εἶχον, ἤθελον, ἐτήρουν, ἐθεώρουν among them. The ambiguity the paradigm shows with λύω is one a reader meets in real verbs.

text: If it begins with a long vowel or a long diphthong there is nothing left to lengthen, so the past looks exactly like the present.
finding: The general rule, and true as far as it goes — Robertson ch.XVIII: the temporal augment is 'often absent, especially with diphthongs'. The example beside it was corrected in this pass, because εὑρίσκω augments three times in seventy-five.

text: This is what makes compound verbs awkward to look up, because the form on the page no longer starts with the letters the lexicon lists.
finding: ἀπέθανεν from ἀποθνῄσκω, with the augment inside. Read and left as written.

text: Two past tenses, and the difference between them is not when the action happened.
finding: The chapter's thesis about aspect, and Huffman Part 2 says the same of tense-form generally: selection is 'based primarily upon the way the author wishes to think about the action'.

text: εὑρίσκω keeps its εὑ- in 72 of its 75 past forms, so the ending is usually the only thing distinguishing the imperfect from the present — the three exceptions augment to ηὕ-.
finding: Was 'εὑρίσκω keeps its εὑ- throughout'. Mostly true and not entirely: of its 75 past-tense forms, 72 keep εὑ- and three augment to ηὑ- — ηὕρισκον at Mark 14:55 and Acts 7:11, and ηὑρίσκετο at Hebrews 11:5, against an unaugmented εὕρισκον at Luke 19:48. So the same verb shows both, which is worth more than the tidy version: Robertson ch.XVIII says the temporal augment is 'often absent, especially with diphthongs' — often, not always. Body and quiz corrected together.

text: Only that it is viewed as a whole, from outside.
finding: The aorist's aspect, stated as narrowly as the chapter's own warning requires. Read and left as written.

text: Its past is the imperfect: ἤμην, ἦς, ἦν, ἦμεν, ἦτε, ἦσαν — and ἦν alone accounts for most of its 455 occurrences.
finding: 455 imperfect indicatives of εἰμί, exact; ἦν is 314 of them = 69%, so 'most' holds. The rest: ἦσαν 95, ἤμην 15, ἦτε 10, ἦμεν 8, ἦς 6, ἤμεθα 5, ἦσθα 2.

text: None of those can be reasoned out.
finding: About principal parts having to be learned. Read and left as written.

text: It does not say the action was quick, or once only, or finished — those are things the sentence may tell you, and the tense does not.
finding: The chapter's central correction about the aorist, and the thing the whole course is built to prevent. Read and left as written; Huffman Part 2 says the same of tense-form generally — selection is about how the author wishes to think about the action, not about the action itself.

text: Singular Plural 1st ἤμην ἦμεν 2nd ἦς ἦτε 3rd ἦν ἦσαν οὗτος ἦν ἐν ἀρχῇ πρὸς τὸν θεόν "He was in the beginning with God." ἦν alone accounts for most of these 455 occurrences, and John 1 uses it to hold a state open rather than to report an event — which is the imperfective aspect doing exactly what this chapter has been describing.
finding: 455 imperfect indicatives of εἰμί, of which ἦν is 314 — 69%.

text: εὑρίσκω keeps its εὑ- almost throughout — 72 of its 75 past forms do — and the ending is then the only thing telling you the tense.
finding: Was 'εὑρίσκω keeps its εὑ- throughout'. Mostly true and not entirely: of its 75 past-tense forms, 72 keep εὑ- and three augment to ηὑ- — ηὕρισκον at Mark 14:55 and Acts 7:11, and ηὑρίσκετο at Hebrews 11:5, against an unaugmented εὕρισκον at Luke 19:48. So the same verb shows both, which is worth more than the tidy version: Robertson ch.XVIII says the temporal augment is 'often absent, especially with diphthongs' — often, not always. Body and quiz corrected together.

text: If the verb already begins with a short vowel, that vowel lengthens instead of taking a prefix: ἀκούω → ἤκουον .

finding: SETTLED, and by chapter 4's own test. It said 'The test is whether the writer could have written it the other way' — so the question at Luke 18:13 is not what τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ means but whether Luke had the option of leaving the article out. Corpus: a dative pronoun with a noun or adjective in apposition occurs 12 times, 8 of them articular, and SEVEN OF THE EIGHT ARE LUKE — ὑμῖν τοῖς πλουσίοις (6:24), ὑμῖν τοῖς Φαρισαίοις (11:42, 11:43), ὑμῖν τοῖς νομικοῖς (11:46, 11:52), ὑμῖν τοῖς φίλοις (12:4), and μοι τῷ ἁμαρτωλῷ itself. None of the other six means 'the Pharisees above all others'; they mean 'you Pharisees'. The eighth is Ephesians 3:8 ἐμοὶ τῷ ἐλαχιστοτέρῳ. So the article is the construction, not a choice, and by the chapter's own rule it is not evidence. Chapter 27 was the sharper case: the sentence immediately before the quotation states the could-have-written-it-otherwise test, and the next sentence breaks it on a presence. Both chapters now say so, and the example is kept — it teaches the fallacy better than it taught the reading.
